source_title: 11 of the Best Financial Advisor Companies: Well-Known Fiduciary Investment Firms to Consider
source_excerpt:
These 11 financial advising firms all receive 4.5 and 5 stars in our ratings.
Top-rated financial advising firms have low fees and offer access to highly credentialed financial advisors and planning professionals.
The best financial advisors work with you based on your goals and offer a fee structure that’s affordable to a range of clients.
The best financial advisors can help you create a comprehensive financial roadmap so you can grow your wealth and reach your goals. One place to start is with a registered investment adviser (RIA) company, as they employ financial advisors who must act as fiduciaries, meaning they have to act in their clients’ best interests.
11 of the best financial advisor companies for 2026
Buy Side reviewed some of the larger and more well-known independent RIAs, and ranked them based on criteria such as advisor credentials and accessibility, fees, available services and asset and portfolio options.
It’s important to note that no matter which financial advisor firm you select, you also must evaluate each individual advisor thoroughly.
Some of the qualities of top-rated financial advisor firms include low fees, accessible account minimums and a high percentage of advisors who are CFPs. You will find more details on our methodology below.
The following financial advisory firms received the highest Buy Side ratings. While all of these firms connect you with a financial advisor, the account minimums and fees for accessing an advisor vary, which we detail below.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.10% to 0.65% AUM
Betterment Premium offers one-on-one access to a financial planning professional as needed if you have at least $100,000 assets under management (AUM). If you’re a hands-off investor who wants access to guidance, Betterment Premium can be an attractive choice. You get all of the benefits of Betterment’s robo advisor with the financial planning services you’d find at other firms. While the minimum AUM is higher than some other firms on our list, it’s low enough to make financial planning and advising more accessible than many wealth management firms.
However, while there is some degree of customization available through a variety of portfolio choices, Betterment Premium doesn’t offer as many alternative assets as some firms, and the portfolios aren’t fully tailored to the client. Similarly, the firm doesn’t have as comprehensive of planning services as many firms offer. Notably, it doesn’t offer estate planning services.
Read Buy Side’s Betterment review to learn more.
Rather than charging based on AUM, Facet Wealth offers membership levels at flat rates. You can choose to pay annually or quarterly. Facet frequently offers discounts on its memberships, so you might not have to pay full price when signing up. For those with more assets in their portfolios, the flat fee can translate into a lower percentage of AUM. Facet offers a full suite of services, but you might only be able to access some features, like extra meetings with an advisor or wealth manager, at the highest tier.
Facet offers investment management in addition to other financial and life planning services. It functions as a one-stop shop for management. However, clients are limited in the assets they have exposure to, with the company mainly utilizing ETFs as part of its strategy and alternative assets mainly in the form of mutual funds that hold private loans and real estate. While Facet only requires a $500 minimum investment, clients with lower account balances will end up paying a considerably higher percentage fee.
Read Buy Side’s Facet review to learn more.
While Retirable appeals to a variety of demographics, the advisory firm focuses heavily on helping soon-to-be and recent retirees manage their income during retirement. Retirable uses a process that involves dynamic income planning to help determine a monthly retirement “paycheck” you can use to cover your basic needs and wants, along with other comprehensive financial planning services. While its advisory fees aren’t among the lowest fees of all firms, its capped fee means that once you hit $1 million, your percentage fee will decrease.
Because its services are tailored to retirees, Retirable likely isn’t a good fit for emerging investors. There are also some limitations with using Retirable. For example, the firm requires that you use its preferred brokerage firm and it doesn’t offer alternative assets in its portfolios.
Read Buy Side’s Retirable review to learn more.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.20% to 1.00% of AUM, with quarterly minimum fees
Modera Wealth Management offers comprehensive wealth management, portfolio management and retirement plan consulting. The firm offers custom portfolios, including access to environmental, social and corporate-governance (ESG) investing and alternative assets, such as private real estate and equity. Additionally, Modera Wealth Management offers special services, including disability planning, and provides planning for LGBTQ individuals. If you have special circumstances, including divorce, Modera Wealth Management might be a good choice.
On the other hand, Modera imposes quarterly fee minimums ranging from $2,500 to $3,000, which might cause those with lower account balances to pay a higher percentage of AUM as a result. Additionally, the firm has less impressive digital tools than some competitors.
If you’re located near one of the firm’s physical offices, you might be able to meet with your advisor in person. Otherwise, you’ll have to meet virtually. Modera has offices in Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.25% to 1.20% of AUM
Creative Planning offers comprehensive financial planning and investment management services to those with at least $200,000 in AUM. Clients of Creative Planning have access to custom portfolios constructed by advisors and wealth managers based on their needs, as well as access to a variety of asset classes. Its robust planning services are tailored to high-net-worth clients and include family office, strategic tax planning and estate planning.
In addition to providing advisory services, Creative Planning also sells some financial products. As a result, some advisors and wealth managers affiliated with this firm are fee-based and not fee-only. The firm has a higher investment minimum than many competitors—you’ll need at least $200,000 in investable assets to become a client. Creative Planning might be attractive to high-net-worth individuals who want financial planning guidance as well as portfolio management.
Read Buy Side’s Creative Planning review to learn more.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.49% to 0.89% of AUM
Empower Personal Strategy offers investment management and financial advice to clients with at least $100,000 in investible assets. It might be an attractive option for clients who want access to a digital dashboard and are looking for increased tax efficiency with their investments at affordable management fees.
At Empower’s lowest tier, you can access unlimited advice from the advisory team and use digital tools to manage your account. However, for features like dedicated advisors and increased planning and portfolio services, you need a much higher account balance. The highest degree of personalized advice and customization is available to those with at least $1 million in investible assets.
Read Buy Side’s Empower review to learn more.
Flat fees ranging from $3,950 to $12,500 per year
Range Advisory offers comprehensive financial planning and investment management for a flat annual fee, with no minimum investment requirement. The firm uses a tech-forward approach, providing a dashboard with planning tools and projections, as well as an AI wealth advisor that you can ask questions to around the clock (while also having access to video calls with a financial advisor, as needed).
Range Advisory uses a team approach to advising—your membership gives you access to a team of credentialed investment and tax professionals. However, you won’t get a dedicated advisor. Additionally, while the flat fee might be attractive for clients with larger account balances, it will be disproportionately high if you have a small balance. For example, with an account balance of $100,000, the $3,950 fee for the lowest service tier works out to 3.95% AUM, several times the industry average.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.60% to 1.25% of AUM
Mariner Wealth Advisors provides wealth management and investment management services to clients with $100,000 or more to invest. It’s a solid option for investors who want customized, diversified portfolios that include alternative investments in addition to traditional stocks, bonds and investment funds. Its comprehensive services include cash flow analysis, savings strategies and tax and estate planning. The firm has offices in most states, meaning many customers can meet with an advisor in person.
Mariner Wealth Advisors comes with a higher price tag for investors with lower account balances. Anyone with less than $1 million under management will pay a 1.25% AUM fee. The firm also charges a quarterly minimum fee of $1,875. For someone with $100,000 under management, that amounts to a 7.50% AUM fee per year.
Read Buy Side’s Mariner review to learn more.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.50% to 1.60% of AUM
Pure Financial Advisors has a team composed almost entirely of CFP professionals who offer financial planning and investment management services. For clients who don’t want to pay the AUM fee—especially those with smaller account balances—the firm offers stand-alone financial planning services starting at $1,000.
It has no minimum investment requirement, meaning you can work with the firm even if you’re just getting started. However, the AUM fee for smaller account balances is well above the industry benchmark. The firm doesn’t offer as much portfolio customization as many others—it uses model portfolios instead. If you want more investment options, including bonds and individual stocks, you might have to pay an additional fee for a sub-advisor.
Read Buy Side’s Pure Financial Advisors review to learn more.
Tiered fees ranging from 0.40% to 0.90% of AUM
NerdWallet Wealth Partners offers wealth planning, investment management and financial coaching services. While the firm primarily works with customers with at least $100,000 in investable assets, it has no account minimum. All of NerdWallet Wealth Partners’ advisors are fiduciaries, meaning they must act in your best interests. Additionally, because advisors don’t accept commissions, there’s less room for conflicts of interest.
Its fees are below the industry benchmark for almost all clients. However, those with less than $100,000 pay a flat fee of $900, which could add up to more than 1% AUM. The firm primarily builds portfolios out of passive investment funds, making them slightly more difficult to customize. Additionally, certain investment strategies, including ESG investing, require working with a sub-advisor, which comes at an additional cost.
Read Buy Side’s NerdWallet Wealth Partners review to learn more.
Up to 2.00% of AUM with $2,500 annual minimum
Allworth Financial offers holistic wealth management from credentialed advisors who coordinate with in-house specialists to ensure your investments, financial plan, tax strategy, insurance needs and estate plan are all aligned. Allworth doesn’t disclose its fee schedule but caps its management fee at 2.00% of AUM, which is higher than the industry average. It also has a minimum annual fee of $2,500. If you have $250,000 in your account, a $2,500 minimum translates to a 1.00% fee.
With Allworth, you can invest in a variety of assets, including the private funds Allworth manages. These private funds have an investment minimum of $250,000. The firm also offers a range of model investment strategies, such as ESG and income-focused strategies.
What services do financial advisors offer?
Financial advisors offer a variety of services, ranging from planning and advice to portfolio management. Not all advisors offer investment management, however.
“Many financial planning professionals focus on helping you create structure and strategy as you go through your financial life,” said Chelsea Ransom-Cooper, CFP and cofounder of Zenith Wealth Partners. “Some financial advisors will manage your portfolio, but many focus on providing practical planning and advice and leave the implementation up to you.”
Depending on the financial advisor, you might also be able to get expert insight in the following areas:
“Financial advisors offer a holistic view of how your money fits into your life and work with you to create a roadmap that provides a clear path forward to meet your money and life goals,” Ransom-Cooper said.
In some cases, a financial advisor might specialize in a specific area, such as retirement or budgeting.
What are the costs associated with hiring a financial advisor?
In general, you pay an advisory fee when you work with a financial advisor, unless they are paid based on commission. A fee-only advisor earns money only from what clients pay them. A fee-based advisor charges fees to the client, but might also earn a commission from financial products they sell, such as insurance.
When comparing the costs of a financial advisor , consider which fee structure makes sense for your situation:
Assets under management: Under this model, your financial advisor charges you based on the assets they manage on your behalf. If the financial advisor doesn’t manage investments, they likely won’t use this fee structure.
Subscription: Some financial planners and advisors charge a monthly or quarterly subscription fee for advice and services. This model is similar to a retainer, but with a subscription or membership, you might get access to self-management tools in addition to a certain number of check-ins and planning sessions.
Retainer: An annual fee paid based on the services you receive. A retainer might be paid monthly, quarterly or annually. Often, you work with your advisor to predetermine the services you receive and the number of appointments you have throughout the year.
Hourly: Some financial advisors charge an hourly rate. You pay based on the number of consultation hours. Additionally, if the advisor performs tasks related to your financial plan, they might charge for those hours as well.
Fixed: This is a flat fee charged for specific services. For example, a financial advisor might charge a flat rate to create a retirement strategy, or they might have a set fee for a 45-minute check-in.
Industry analysis firm Envestnet points out that AUM is the most common fee structure, and the average is 0.96%. The next most common structure is a flat fee, with an average cost of $2,926. Other fee structures are much less common, but it’s typical to pay an average of $307 an hour or expect to pay a monthly subscription fee of $595.
Some advisors charge a combination of fees. For example, an advisor might charge you an AUM fee for portfolio management, but then list a flat rate for creating a comprehensive education plan.
Pay attention to tiered fees as well. In many cases, as your account balance grows, you pay a lower percentage of AUM. Financial advisors can have multiple tiers, so make sure you understand when you reach a new threshold. For example, you might pay 0.65% on the first million under management, and then pay a lower rate of 0.45% on assets above that amount. So, if you have $2 million in assets, you would pay $6,500 on the first million and $4,500 on the $1 million above that initial threshold. With that structure, you would pay $11,000 in AUM fees.
Finally, find out if your financial advisor firm has a minimum fee requirement. The AUM percentage might seem reasonable, but if you have a relatively small balance with the firm, and there’s a flat quarterly minimum, your actual percentage might be higher. For example, if a firm charges an annual fee of 0.96% AUM and a quarterly minimum of $1,500 ($6,000 annually), a client with $100,000 under management would pay significantly more than the $960 that’s the 0.96% of their assets. Because of the $1,500 quarterly minimum, they would actually end up paying a 6% fee on their assets.
“Most advisors offer a free discovery meeting,” said Zina Kumok, a financial advisor at C.H. Douglas & Gray Wealth Management. “Find out how they charge and how they work, and make sure you understand what they offer for the price you’re paying.”
How to choose the right financial advisor for your needs
One of the frustrations that would-be clients often encounter is the fact that there are so many terms and titles used by financial professionals.
“All these terms—financial advisor, retirement advisor, wealth manager, coach—can be a mess for the consumer to understand,” said Roger Whitney, CFP and co-founder of Retire Agile. “Figure out what you want from the advisor in the first place. Start with what you need help with and what you want to accomplish.”
Whitney suggests that a good place to start when choosing a financial advisor is finding someone with a certified financial planner (CFP) designation who has the education and experience to provide insight into various aspects of financial planning at different life stages.
The CFP designation is rigorous and requires education in a broad swath of financial planning topics, and candidates must pass an exam. Additionally, there are experience hours and continuing education requirements to maintain the CFP. Other designations also include education and experience, but the CFP offers a solid foundation and shows a basic understanding of financial planning and advising, Whitney points out.
Other credentials also might help you find an advisor who has increased education and experience in a specific area of need:
Chartered financial analyst (CFA): Advisors must fulfill specific work experience requirements, complete courses and pass three exams set forth by the CFA Institute. This designation includes extra education on investment analysis and portfolio management.
Accredited financial counselor (AFC): Requires experience hours and an education course, as well as passing an exam. Often, these professionals help clients with financial basics such as debt reduction, saving and understanding the connection between money and emotions. To remain credentialed, an advisor must meet ongoing education requirements set forth by the Association for Financial Counseling and Planning Education.
Chartered financial consultant (ChFC): Generalized and specialized courses are required to receive this designation, as well as ongoing education and adherence to the ethics standards set forth by the American College of Financial Services.
Registered investment adviser (RIA): Registered investment advisers are those who meet specific requirements set by the state or the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This is the only registration that comes with regulatory stipulations, and it can apply to individuals as well as firms.
Certified private wealth advisor (CPWA): Advisors who meet the education and experience requirements put forth by the Investments and Wealth Institute and adhere to ongoing requirements receive this designation, which indicates advanced knowledge of wealth management for high-net-worth individuals.
Retirement income certified professional (RICP): This credential focuses on retirement income planning. It requires courses and ongoing certification through the American College of Financial Services.
If you want help with investments, even if your advisor doesn’t manage your portfolio, Kumok suggests looking for an RIA or someone who works for an RIA firm.
“You know they’re a fiduciary in that case, and you know it’s a regulated designation,” Kumok said.
Many experts emphasize the importance of finding someone who will act as a fiduciary financial advisor. This ensures that they will put your best interests first, regardless of whether it’s best for their own bottom line or their firm’s.
Ransom-Cooper recommends reviewing the credentials of an advisor to determine whether they’re meeting the requirements to be a fiduciary. Complaints against RIAs registered with the SEC are publicly available, and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (Finra) offers its BrokerCheck tool that includes regulatory actions against advisors.
“The CFP Board enforces ethical and fiduciary standards for planners with that designation,” Ransom-Cooper said. “The Board can remove credentials and publicly sanction advisors that don’t meet the requirements.”
There are several reputable online financial advisor directories that can help you find a highly experienced financial advisor, including the National Association of Personal Finance Advisors (NAPFA) financial advisor search tool and the CFP Board ’s CFP professional search tool.
Once you find a few advisors or firms you like, review their websites and read client reviews to learn more about what it’s like to work with them. Narrow your options down to a few advisors and, from there, compare their services, costs, fee structures and anything else that’s important to you. You might also want to consider interviewing your top selections so you can ask specific questions and determine if you have rapport with them. Some of the topics you can inquire about include making sure they offer in-person meetings, have the services you need, are in your budget and are located within the specific mile radius you prefer.
What criteria define a top financial advisor?
The best financial advisor is one who meets your specific needs and budget. Since each person has different financial goals, the criteria that define a top financial advisor are different for everyone. However, a few features help financial advisors stand out among the rest, no matter the client. Top financial advisors are often fiduciaries, meaning they are held to higher standards and have a legal obligation to act in their client’s best interest. Top advisors also carry credentials that are applicable to your needs, provide excellent customer service and offer a range of products and services.
What minimum assets should I have before hiring a top‑tier advisor?
Many advisors require a minimum amount of assets to work with them, and that number varies. For example, while Facet requires a minimum of $500 to work with an advisor and start investing, Betterment requires a minimum of $100,000 to meet with a financial advisor. The type of advisor and plan you choose might also influence the minimum assets you should have. Betterment requires $10 in assets for its robo-advising service, but doesn’t provide access to a financial advisor. You might also incur a monthly charge if your assets are below a certain amount.
Top-tier advisors tend to be more exclusive, provide additional services and often handle complex finances. They might take a more holistic approach to your finances overall, not just investments. They might also specialize in specific areas like estate planning and taxes or connect you with other experts who can help. Because of this, you’ll likely see higher minimum asset requirements that can range from hundreds of thousands of dollars to more than a million.
How often should I review my advisor’s performance and fit?
Financial needs and goals can change, so it’s important to review your advisor’s performance at least once per year to make sure their services still meet your needs. However, there are certain situations in which it might be wise to do semi-annual or quarterly reviews instead:
You’re a high-net-worth individual, meaning you have more than $1 million in assets.
You have multiple income streams, or your financial situation is more complex than the average client.
